title: The Dead on the Roster
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 7 of 40
content:
The dead had lockers.

That was what bothered me most.

Not the casualty list. Lists were abstract. Ink did not smell like anyone. Names written in a column could be folded, filed, copied into a report.

Lockers were different.

Knight Brach had left a deck of cards tied with a red string. Worwick had three spare socks, one with a badly repaired heel. Dawes kept a tin of peppermints that had fused together with age and heat. Keane’s locker contained a photograph so faded I could not make out the faces.

The station was too small to let the dead disappear politely.

I found Danse standing in front of the open row after midnight.

He was out of armor, wearing a dark shirt with the sleeves pushed to his forearms. A bottle of beer sat unopened on the bench beside him.

I almost backed away.

He spoke without turning.

“You can come in.”

“Thought you were asleep.”

“So did I.”

I leaned against the doorway.

The garage light buzzed overhead.

Danse held something small in one hand.

A Brotherhood holotag.

“Whose?” I asked.

“Brach.”

He rubbed his thumb over the stamped letters.

“We attacked a raider position at Corvega. I thought we could force them out and secure the plant.”

His voice had the flat quality people used when telling a story they had already told themselves too many times.

“Worwick took a round during the retreat. Brach stepped on a mine trying to get him clear.”

I said nothing.

“He died in three minutes.”

The details were too precise.

I knew then that Danse had counted them.

“Worwick held on two days.”

He placed the tag on the bench.

“Dawes was killed at Fort Strong. Keane…”

“Cambridge.”

“Yes.”

His jaw flexed.

“Four soldiers. More than half the squad I brought here.”

“You didn’t kill them.”

“I made the decisions that put them there.”

“You made decisions in a place where every option can get someone killed.”

“That doesn’t absolve command.”

“I didn’t say it did.”

He finally looked at me.

There was anger in his face, but not at me.

“Then what are you saying?”

“That responsibility and guilt aren’t always the same thing.”

His expression hardened.

“That sounds convenient.”

“It sounds true.”

“If I start deciding none of it was my fault, what happens the next time?”

“You learn from it.”

“I already did.”

“Then why are you standing here at midnight punishing yourself?”

The question landed.

Danse looked away.

For a while the only sound was the generator outside cycling under load.

“I should have withdrawn from Corvega sooner.”

“Maybe.”

His eyes snapped back to me.

“You agree?”

“I wasn’t there.”

“Then why say maybe?”

“Because I’m not going to comfort you by pretending commanders never make bad calls.”

That stopped him more effectively than kindness would have.

I pushed away from the doorway and sat on the bench, leaving space between us.

“Maybe you made mistakes. Maybe you didn’t. Either way, those men were soldiers, not furniture you moved into danger. They had choices too.”

Danse stared at the locker doors.

“Brach trusted me.”

“Then honor the trust by becoming better, not by convincing yourself he died because you’re secretly poison.”

He was quiet long enough that I wondered if I had gone too far.

Then he sat beside me.

The bench creaked under his weight.

“I don’t think I’m poison.”

“Good.”

“I think you’re dramatic.”

“There he is.”

His mouth almost smiled.

Almost.

I picked up the beer.

“You going to drink this?”

“I was considering it.”

“Very decisive.”

He took it from me, twisted the cap off, and drank.

“You want one?”

“Are you offering me contraband on duty?”

“I’m off duty.”

“Are you ever?”

That made him pause.

“No,” he said after a moment. “Probably not.”

He retrieved a second bottle from a crate.

We sat under the buzzing light and drank warm beer among the belongings of dead soldiers.

It should have been morbid.

Instead it felt like a vigil.

After a while Danse told me something about Keane always losing gloves. Then a story about Dawes beating Rhys in cards three nights in a row and refusing to reveal how. Then how Worwick snored loudly enough to be a tactical liability.

Each memory put flesh back onto the names.

I listened.

Eventually he reached Brach.

The words stopped.

“He was young,” Danse said.

“How young?”

“Young enough that I should have known better.”

“That isn’t an age.”

“No.”

He rolled the empty bottle between his hands.

“I keep thinking if I remember every detail, I won’t make the same mistake.”

“And does it work?”

“I don’t know.”

That might have been the first time I heard him admit uncertainty without fighting it.

I let the silence sit.

Danse looked over.

“Why are you still here?”

“At the station?”

“Yes.”

“I like Haylen.”

“Very funny.”

“I like the workbench.”

He waited.

I sighed.

“You people looked like you needed help.”

“That’s not the whole answer.”

“Look who suddenly notices evasive responses.”

“I always notice.”

I looked down at my beer.

The whole answer was not something I had language for yet.

The station felt less lonely than the road.

Haylen had begun leaving scavenged technical magazines beside my bedroll. Rhys complained when I borrowed his cleaning solvent but always left the bottle where I could find it. Danse made awful coffee and corrected my shooting stance and watched doors instead of pockets.

It had become dangerously easy to imagine staying.

“I don’t know,” I said.

Danse considered that.

Then nodded.

“Fair.”

We finished the beers.

Before he closed the lockers, Danse placed each small object back exactly where he had found it.

Cards. Socks. Peppermints. Photograph.

Before he did, he picked up the red-stringed deck of cards and turned it over once in his hands.

“Brach marked the queens,” he said.

“With what?”

“A thumbnail scratch on the corner.”

I examined the top card. The mark was so small I would never have noticed it.

“You still caught him cheating?”

“Eventually.”

“Eventually?”

Danse gave me a look.

“He was very good at probability.”

I laughed. The sound felt almost disrespectful in the quiet garage until Danse smiled too.

That was the point, I realized. Mourning did not have to flatten the dead into solemn portraits. Brach could be brave and irritating. Worwick could sing badly. Keane could own a baseball card. Remembering their worst jokes did not diminish the way they died.

It gave them back something death had taken.

He shut Brach’s last.

His hand stayed on the metal door.

“I appreciate you listening.”

I stood beside him.

“Any time.”

He looked at me.

Something in his face made my chest tighten.

Not romance. Not yet.

Trust, perhaps.

The first fragile layer of it.

For Danse, I suspected that was more dangerous than attraction would ever be.

He switched off the light.

We walked back into the station together, leaving the dead where they belonged: remembered, but not alone.

The next evening I found Danse replacing the tape that held the casualty list to the wall.

The old adhesive had curled in the humidity. One corner kept lifting.

He pressed it flat with his thumb.

It peeled back again.

“You know there are easier materials to fight,” I said from the doorway.

“I’m aware.”

I handed him a strip of fresh cloth tape.

He accepted it without comment.

This time the paper stayed.

Brach. Worwick. Dawes. Keane.

Four names that had been scenery the first day I walked into the station.

They were not scenery anymore.

“Tell me one thing about each of them,” I said.

Danse went still.

I almost took it back.

Then he looked at the first name.

“Knight Brach cheated at cards.”

I blinked.

“That wasn’t what I expected.”

“He claimed he was counting probabilities.”

“Was he?”

“He was hiding cards in his sleeve.”

A faint smile touched Danse’s mouth.

He moved to the second.

“Knight Worwick sang.”

“Good?”

“No.”

“Enthusiastically?”

“Constantly.”

The smile deepened.

“Dawes could repair nearly anything provided nobody asked him to explain how. Keane…”

The smile disappeared.

Danse folded his arms.

“Keane was the youngest. He kept a collection of pre-War baseball cards even though he didn’t understand the game.”

“Did you?”

“No.”

“Did anyone?”

“Haylen pretended to.”

From the next room Haylen called, “I heard that.”

Danse raised his voice. “Then you also heard that your explanation of a designated hitter was incoherent.”

“It was perfectly coherent!”

I laughed.

For one breath, the station contained the shape of the people it had lost. Not as bodies. As cheaters and bad singers and mechanics and a kid carrying pictures of a game nobody remembered how to play.

Danse’s expression changed when he realized what had happened.

“You did that deliberately.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because a list can start feeling like a tally.”

His gaze returned to the names.

“I keep it so I don’t forget.”

“I know.”

“That is my responsibility.”

“Remembering them?”

“Remembering why they died.”

There it was. The blade beneath the grief.

I stepped beside him.

“You can remember who they were too.”

His throat moved.

“That may be more difficult.”

“Most worthwhile things are.”

He glanced at me.

“That sounded like something from a Brotherhood field manual.”

“God, no.”

The laugh escaped him before he could stop it.

Haylen laughed from the other room too.

Danse shook his head.

But he left the list on the wall.

And below it, tucked beneath the fresh tape, he placed one of Keane’s battered baseball cards.
